content: Vitiligo is a chronic skin condition characterized by the loss of pigment, leading to irregular, pale patches on the skin. The exact cause of vitiligo is not fully understood, but it is believed to result from a combination of autoimmune, genetic, and environmental factors. It is the most common depigmenting disorder, affecting approximately 1% of the global population. The history of vitiligo dates back over 3,000 years, with descriptions of similar conditions found in ancient texts such as the Eber Papyrus, the Atharva Veda, and the Bible. These texts reference white-spotted diseases that may include cases of vitiligo. The histopathological features of vitiligo were first described by C. and Moriz Kaposi. Vitiligo can be classified into two clinical subtypes: segmental vitiligo, which affects only one segment of the body (e.g., the face, arm, or leg), and non-segmental vitiligo, which involves more than one segment, such as both knees or both hands. The condition is caused by the loss of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells in the skin. While the exact mechanism is unknown, an autoimmune process is thought to play a role in some cases. This hypothesis is supported by the higher prevalence of vitiligo in individuals with autoimmune disorders such as Addison's disease, hyperthyroidism, alopecia areata, and pernicious anemia. However, it is important to note that most individuals with vitiligo do not have any associated autoimmune conditions. Vitiligo must be differentiated from other conditions that cause hypopigmentation, such as pityriasis alba, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, tinea versicolor, halo nevus, tuberous sclerosis, and albinism. Epidemiologically, vitiligo affects males and females equally, with a prevalence of 1% in the general population. Half of the cases are diagnosed before the age of 20. Risk factors include a family history of vitiligo and the presence of autoimmune diseases. Individuals with a relative affected by vitiligo have an 18-fold increased risk of developing the condition, often with an earlier onset. The natural course of vitiligo is variable. Depigmentation may remain stable, progress to total body depigmentation, or, in rare cases, remit spontaneously. Spontaneous remission, however, is uncommon. Vitiligo is typically asymptomatic and often presents during the second decade of life, with gradual depigmentation over time. On physical examination, the condition manifests as irregular, pale patches of skin distributed in various patterns. There are no specific laboratory abnormalities associated with vitiligo. However, laboratory tests may be ordered to rule out associated conditions such as pernicious anemia, Addison's disease, and thyroid disorders. In some cases, a biopsy of the affected skin may reveal microscopic changes in the hypopigmented region, although this is not routinely performed. Treatment options for vitiligo include medical therapies such as potent topical corticosteroids (e.g., mometasone) and topical calcineurin inhibitors, which are considered first-line treatments to achieve repigmentation. Phototherapy has also been shown to be effective for generalized vitiligo. Combined treatment with topical calcineurin inhibitors and phototherapy has demonstrated greater efficacy in achieving repigmentation in a shorter period compared to single treatments. Support groups and organizations play a crucial role in helping individuals with vitiligo understand their condition, explore treatment options, and connect with others facing similar challenges. Notable organizations include: Vitiligo Support International: The largest vitiligo organization globally, offering free access to online message boards, chat rooms, FAQs, articles, and a patient-referred doctor search. The group also advocates for patients, conducts conferences, and organizes local support groups. The National Vitiligo Foundation (NVF): A nonprofit organization providing online resources, physician listings, and FAQs. It funds research through grants and sponsors local support groups and workshops. The American Vitiligo Research Foundation Inc. (AVRF): A nonprofit charity focused on increasing public awareness of vitiligo and supporting affected individuals, particularly children and their families. The organization also supports research into alternative methods for finding a cure. VITFriends, LLC: A support group based in the Northeastern United States, formed in 2004. It offers encouragement and hope to individuals with vitiligo and aims to raise public awareness about the condition.
